learning_objective: 🎯 Understand the 'machine' that is your body! Learn how anatomy, physiology, and physics (biomechanics) work together to create athletic champions.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Anatomy is the study of the structure of the human body (bones, muscles). Physiology is the study of how these parts function. Knowing this helps athletes train specific muscles and avoid injuries.
Regular exercise increases lung capacity (more oxygen intake) and stroke volume (the amount of blood the heart pumps in one beat). This builds high stamina and endurance.
Muscles pull on bones to create movement. There are two main types of muscle fibers: Slow-twitch (red fibers, good for marathons) and Fast-twitch (white fibers, good for sprinting/weightlifting).

This applies the laws of physics to human movement. It studies forces, friction, and angles. For example, biomechanics teaches a javelin thrower the exact angle (around 45 degrees) to throw for maximum distance.
The scientific study of human body movement. It helps in evaluating the quality of movement, improving athletic performance, and aiding in physical rehabilitation.

fun_activity.title: 📐 The Optimal Angle Test
fun_activity.instructions: Take a small crumpled paper ball. Throw it forward three times: once aiming low (flat), once aiming very high (steep), and once aiming in the middle (about 45 degrees). Notice which throw travels the farthest distance. You just used Biomechanics!

exam_tips: 📌 Clearly differentiate between Anatomy (structure) and Physiology (function).
📌 Remember the difference between slow-twitch fibers (endurance/marathon) and fast-twitch fibers (speed/power).
📌 Define Biomechanics and give one practical example of how it improves sports performance.
quick_recap: ⭐ The human skeleton provides the levers, and muscles provide the force to move them.
⭐ An athlete's resting heart rate is much lower than a normal person's because their heart is stronger.
⭐ Friction is a necessary force in sports—spikes on running shoes increase friction to prevent slipping.
